entry: Grand Duke of Lithuania (1401–1430), who first ruled as regent for his cousin [[Władysław II Jagiełło|Jogaila]] (1392–1401). In 1381 Vytautas' father, Kęstutis, seized [[Vilnius]] and imprisoned Jogaila, but Kęstutis and Vytautas were then arrested and taken to Kreva Castle. Kęstutis was found dead a week later; whether he died of natural causes or was murdered is still debated. Vytautas escaped in 1382 and sought help from the [[Teutonic Order]], breaking with the Order and reconciling with Jogaila in 1384. He regained his father's lands except Trakai and claimed the titles King of the Hussites and King of Lithuania. In 1392 Jogaila offered him the regency, and Vytautas again broke with the Order. In modern Lithuania he is revered as a national hero, and Vytautas Magnus University was named for him in commemoration of the 500-year anniversary of his death.

American professional wrestling and entertainment company based in Stamford, [[Connecticut]]. It traces its origins to the Capitol Wrestling Corporation, formed in 1953, which became the World Wrestling Federation in 1979 and World Wrestling Entertainment in 2002. Titan Sports, founded by [[Vince McMahon]] and Linda McMahon, acquired the company in 1982, and WrestleMania grew into the world's largest annual professional wrestling event. WWE markets its product as "sports entertainment." In 2023 WWE merged with Zuffa, parent of the [[Ultimate Fighting Championship]], to form TKO Group Holdings.

Irish poet, dramatist and literary critic, a leading figure in the Irish Literary Revival. With John Millington Synge and Lady Gregory he founded the Abbey Theatre, serving as its chief during its early years. His early verse drew on Irish legend and the [[Occult|occult]] and was influenced by [[John Keats]], [[William Wordsworth]] and [[William Blake]]; his first volume appeared in 1889. From 1900 his poetry became more rooted in the physical world, realistic and politicized, and he promoted younger poets such as [[Ezra Pound]]. Major works include *The Land of Heart's Desire* (1894), *Cathleen ni Houlihan* (1902), *The Wild Swans at Coole* (1919) and *The Tower* (1928). He received the 1923 Nobel Prize in Literature and served two terms as a senator of the Irish Free State.

British evolutionary biologist. His theoretical work gave a rigorous genetic basis for altruism, an insight central to the gene-centered view of evolution, and he is considered a forerunner of sociobiology. His two 1964 papers, "The Genetical Evolution of Social Behaviour," introduced Hamilton's rule: a costly action should be performed when the benefit to the recipient, weighted by the genetic relatedness of actor and recipient, outweighs the cost to the actor. The key quantity in his calculations was Sewall Wright's coefficient of relationship. He also did important work on sex ratios and the evolution of sex. He studied at the [[University of Cambridge]] and from 1984 was a Royal Society Research Professor at Oxford University. [[Richard Dawkins]] has written that Hamilton was "the greatest Darwinian of my lifetime."

American sociologist, historian and Pan-Africanist civil rights activist. The first African American to earn a doctorate at [[Harvard University]], he taught at Atlanta University and was a prolific author who protested lynching, Jim Crow laws and racial discrimination. He led the Niagara Movement, which demanded full civil rights, and argued that an educated "talented tenth" should lead racial uplift. He helped found the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) in 1909 and edited its journal *The Crisis*. *The Souls of Black Folk* is a seminal work of African American literature, and *Black Reconstruction in America* (1935) challenged the view that Black Americans were responsible for the failures of the Reconstruction era. He popularized the phrase "color line," borrowed from [[Frederick Douglass]]. After World War II he was targeted by the [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]]. He spent his last years in [[Ghana]].

English cricketer and medical practitioner, widely held to be one of the greatest players of [[Cricket|cricket]]. Known as "WG," he played first-class cricket for a record-equaling 44 seasons, from 1865 to 1908, mostly for Gloucestershire, the Gentlemen, and Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC). He is regarded as the originator of modern batsmanship and generally captained the teams he represented at all levels. He represented England in 22 Test matches from 1880 to 1899. In 1880 he and his brothers Edward and Fred were members of the same England team, the first time three brothers played together in a Test match. Grace nominally remained an amateur, but he was said to have made more money from cricket than any contemporary professional. He qualified as a doctor in 1879 and later took up [[Golf]], [[Curling]] and lawn bowls.

Grand Duke of Lithuania from 1377 and King of Poland (1386–1434), born Jogaila. He was the last pagan ruler of medieval Lithuania. Under the Union of Krewo (1385) he pledged to convert to Christianity and marry the child queen Jadwiga of Poland. He was baptized as Ladislaus (Władysław) in [[Kraków]] and crowned King of Poland, and in 1387 he converted Lithuania to Catholicism. His reign laid the foundation for the centuries-long Polish–Lithuanian union, and the Jagiellonian dynasty, which bears his name, ruled both states until 1572. In 1410 the allied Polish and Lithuanian forces, commanded alongside his cousin [[Vytautas the Great]], defeated the [[Teutonic Order]] at the Battle of Grunwald. The Peace of Thorn that followed secured the borders, and his reign extended Polish frontiers, often considered the beginning of Poland's Golden Age.

Vector bosons that mediate the [[Weak interaction|weak interaction]]. The W+ and W− bosons carry an electric charge of +1 and −1 elementary charge and are each other's antiparticles, while the Z0 boson is electrically neutral and is its own antiparticle. All three have spin 1 and are very short-lived, with a half-life of about 3×10⁻²⁵ s. The W boson's mass is 80.3692±0.0133 GeV and the Z boson's is 91.1880±0.0020 GeV. Their high masses limit the range of the weak interaction, in contrast to the massless [[Photon|photon]]. The W bosons are best known for their role in [[Beta decay|beta decay]], in which a neutron is converted into a proton while emitting an electron. The Z boson transfers momentum, spin and energy when [[Neutrino|neutrinos]] scatter from matter, without changing electric charge. Their discovery at [[CERN]] in 1983 was pivotal in establishing the [[Standard Model]] of particle physics.

1993 U.S. law enforcement siege of the Branch Davidians, led by [[David Koresh]], near Waco, [[Texas]]. A Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms raid on February 28 led to a gunfight killing four agents and six Davidians. The [[Federal Bureau of Investigation]] besieged the compound for 51 days. On April 19 a CS gas attack led to a fire that killed 76 Davidians, including 20–28 children and Koresh. Justice Department reports blamed the Davidians for the fire, but critics argue live rounds were fired. [[Timothy McVeigh]] cited the siege as a reason for the [[Oklahoma City bombing]] two years later.

Payment by an employer to an employee for labor. Wages, the [[Price|price]] of labor, are a business expense owed regardless of a company's profitability. They include minimum wages, prevailing wages, yearly bonuses and tip payouts. Wages contrast with salaried work, paid in fixed amounts at regular intervals regardless of hours worked, with commission, which depends on individual performance, and with compensation based on a company's overall performance. Wage labor exchanges money for time at work; the invention of [[Clock|clocks]] coincided with dividing working time, and the [[Hour|hour]] became the most common unit. Wages were paid in Egypt's Middle Kingdom, in [[Ancient Greece|ancient Greece]] and in ancient Rome. Wage rates are shaped by [[Supply and demand|supply and demand]], labor organization, legislation and tradition, and pay differences by sex and race persist in many countries. In [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomics]], the term sometimes covers all monetary employee compensation.

Russian state-funded private military company, controlled until 2023 by Yevgeny Prigozhin, a former close ally of [[Vladimir Putin]]. It helped Russian separatists in [[Donbas]] from 2014 to 2015 and later recruited Russian prison inmates for frontline combat in Ukraine, growing from 1,000 to between 20,000 and 50,000 fighters by the end of 2022. The group also supported regimes in Syria, Libya, the [[Central African Republic]] and [[Mali]], and it has been accused of war crimes against civilians. On June 23, 2023, Prigozhin led an armed rebellion that seized [[Rostov-on-Don]] before halting the next day.

Tragicomedy in two acts by Irish playwright [[Samuel Beckett]]. Written in French as *En attendant Godot* in 1948–1949, the play was first performed in January 1953 at the Théâtre de Babylone in Paris, directed by Roger Blin. Two tramps, Vladimir and Estragon, wait beside a leafless tree for Godot, who never arrives. They encounter Pozzo, his servant Lucky and a boy who brings word that Godot will come "tomorrow," and their repetitive routines suggest the cyclical nature of their lives. Beckett cited [[Caspar David Friedrich]]'s 1819 painting *Two Men Contemplating the Moon* as a major inspiration. Critic Martin Esslin linked the play to the Theatre of the Absurd, a term first proposed by [[Albert Camus]]. A 1998 poll by London's Royal National Theatre named it "the most significant English-language play of the 20th century," and it has been adapted across most of [[Europe]] and the [[Americas]].

Coral atoll in the [[Micronesia]] subregion of the [[Pacific Ocean]], a U.S. unincorporated territory. The United States claimed it in 1899, and [[Pan Am|Pan American Airways]] built an airfield and hotel there in 1935, making it a stopover for trans-Pacific flying boats. Japan occupied it from December 1941 until September 1945. Pan American Airways stopped using the island in 1972, after switching to [[Boeing 747]] aircraft that could cross the ocean without stopping, and the U.S. Air Force took over its administration. About 300 people, mostly military personnel and contractors, are on the island at any given time.

Country that is part of the [[United Kingdom]], occupying the western portion of the island of [[Great Britain]]. Its population was 3.1 million in 2021, and its capital and largest city is [[Cardiff]]. Largely mountainous, Wales has its highest peaks in the north and center, including Snowdon, its highest summit. A distinct Welsh culture emerged among the Celtic Britons after the Roman withdrawal, and Wales was briefly united under Gruffudd ap Llywelyn in 1055. After over 200 years of war, King [[Edward I]] of England completed the conquest, and Owain Glyndŵr led a revolt in the early 15th century. Under the Laws in Wales Acts of 1535 and 1542, Wales was annexed by England and incorporated into its legal system. Coal and metal industries transformed the country during the [[Industrial Revolution]], and two-thirds of the population live in South Wales. [[Welsh language|Welsh]] and English are official languages; 538,300 people speak Welsh.

Conceptual model of air flow in the tropical lower [[Atmospheric circulation|atmosphere]], also called the Walker cell. In this model air parcels follow a closed circulation in the zonal and vertical directions, driven by differences in heat distribution between ocean and land. It is associated with a pressure gradient between a high-pressure system over the eastern [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific]] and a low-pressure system over Indonesia. From an oceanographic point of view, the equatorial cold tongue is caused by easterly winds. As originally proposed, the circulation weakens during El Niño events, when the temperature gradient across the Pacific and the easterlies are reduced, and strengthens during La Niña events. The name honors Gilbert Walker, who discovered the Southern Oscillation in the early 20th century while studying the Indian Ocean [[Monsoon|monsoon]], whose failed rains had caused severe [[Famine|famine]] in 1899. Norwegian-American meteorologist Jacob Bjerknes first used the term in 1969.

Main gait of terrestrial locomotion among legged animals, typically slower than [[Running|running]]. Walking is defined as an "inverted pendulum" gait in which the body vaults over stiff limbs with each step, a pattern shared by arthropods with six, eight or more limbs. In humans, walking differs from running in that only one foot at a time leaves the ground, with a period of double support, while running begins when both feet leave the ground. The average human walking speed at crosswalks is about 5.0 km/h (3.1 mph), and champion racewalkers can average more than 14 km/h over 20 km. An average child walks independently at around 11 months old. Limited research suggests walking may be associated with reduced risk of disease and premature death. In the United Kingdom and Republic of Ireland, "walking" is also synonymous with [[Hiking|hiking]].

Vertical structure, usually solid, that defines or protects an area. Walls carry loads and provide security, shelter, soundproofing or decoration. Types include border barriers between countries, brick walls, [[Defensive wall|defensive walls]] in fortifications and retaining walls that hold back dirt, stone, water or noise. In buildings, walls support roofs, floors and ceilings, enclose spaces and may house [[Electrical wiring|electrical wiring]] or [[Plumbing|plumbing]]. Framed walls transfer loads to the [[Foundation (engineering)|foundation]] through posts, columns or studs, while mass-walls are solid materials such as masonry, concrete, adobe or rammed earth. Walls must conform to local building and fire codes. The word originally referred to defensive walls and ramparts, from the [[Latin]] *vallum*. Famous examples include the [[Great Wall of China]] and [[Hadrian's Wall]], and walls are also used for mosaics and murals.

Street in the Financial District of Lower [[Manhattan]], New York City, running eight city blocks to the East River. Dutch settlers called it *Het Cingel* ("the Belt"), and an actual city wall stood on the street from 1653 to 1699. In the 18th century it was a slave market and securities trading site. The name has become a metonym for the [[New York Stock Exchange]] and the U.S. financial industry. The street is home to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, commercial banks and insurance companies. 40 Wall Street was once the world's tallest building.

Stock market crash in the United States, beginning in October 1929 with a sharp fall in prices on the [[New York Stock Exchange]]. It triggered a rapid erosion of confidence in the U.S. banking system and cascaded into the [[Great Depression]], which lasted until the United States entered [[World War II]] on December 8, 1941. Its most notable days were "Black Thursday," October 24, 1929, when a record 12.9 million shares were traded, and "Black Tuesday," October 29, 1929, when some 16.4 million shares changed hands. Speculation in the [[Roaring Twenties]] had pushed prices far above underlying value, and the market lost some 90% of its pre-crash value before the decline ended on July 8, 1932. Congress responded with the Banking Act of 1933, which separated commercial and investment banking, and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which created the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Scholars disagree about the crash's role in the Great Depression.

Small or middle-sized macropod native to Australia and New Guinea, with introduced populations in [[New Zealand]], [[Hawaii]] and the [[United Kingdom]]. Wallabies belong to the same family as [[Kangaroo|kangaroos]], a name that refers only to the four largest species. The dwarf wallaby, a brush wallaby from New Guinea, is the smallest known wallaby, at about 46 cm long and 1.6 kg. The 19 known rock-wallabies live among rocks, usually near water. The [[Quokka|quokka]] survives on two offshore islands of Western Australia that are free of introduced predators. Wallabies are hunted for meat and fur.

British claymation comedy franchise created by Nick Park and produced by Aardman Animations. It follows Wallace, a cheese-loving inventor, and Gromit, his loyal and intelligent dog, who communicates without dialogue. The first short film, *A Grand Day Out*, was released in 1989. *The Wrong Trousers* (1993) and *A Close Shave* (1995) won [[Academy Awards|Academy Awards]] for Best Animated Short Film, and *Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit* (2005) won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. The franchise has received seven BAFTAs, three Academy Awards and a Peabody Award. The spin-off *Shaun the Sheep* debuted in 2007.

Geographic region of modern Romania and one of two historical principalities that laid the foundation for the modern Romanian state. It lies north of the [[Danube|Lower Danube]] and south of the Southern Carpathians. Wallachia began to form as a principality around the 13th century, and by 1330 Basarab I had defeated the [[Kingdom of Hungary]] at the Battle of Posada. In 1417 it accepted [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]] suzerainty for the first time, a status that lasted until the mid-19th century. Wallachia generally kept its autonomy, though rulers such as [[Vlad the Impaler]] and Michael the Brave interrupted Ottoman rule. In 1859 it united with [[Moldavia]] to form the United Principalities, which adopted the name Romania in 1866. The name Wallachia is an exonym; Romanians called the land *Țara Românească*, "the Romanian Land." After 1918 the Kingdom of Romania also received [[Transylvania]].

Flat case or pouch used to carry small personal items such as currency, debit and [[Credit card|credit cards]], identification and photographs. Wallets are usually made of fabric or leather and are pocket-sized and foldable. They may include a money clip, coin purse, zipper or strap, and specialized versions hold passports or checkbooks. The word originated in late 14th-century English, meaning "bag" or "knapsack," and the modern meaning of a flat case for paper money is first recorded in 1834 in American English. The ancient Greek *kibisis*, the pouch carried by [[Hermes]] and the sack in which [[Perseus]] carried the severed head of [[Medusa]], is typically translated as "wallet." Wallets developed after paper currency reached the West in the 1600s, and the modern bi-fold wallet with multiple card slots was standardized in the early 1950s with the introduction of the first credit cards.

French overseas collectivity in the South Pacific, lying between [[Tuvalu]], [[Fiji]], [[Tonga]], [[Samoa]] and [[Tokelau]]. It consists of the Wallis Islands (Uvea) and the Hoorn Islands (Futuna and Alofi), about 260 km apart. It became a French overseas collectivity on March 28, 2003, and is an overseas country and territory of the [[European Union]]. Its population was 11,151 at the July 2023 census, down from 14,944 in 2003. [[Lapita culture|Lapita]] artifacts date the earliest habitation to between 850 and 800 BCE, and French missionaries from 1837 converted the population to Roman Catholicism.

Southernmost of the three federal regions of [[Belgium]], primarily French-speaking. It covers 55% of Belgium's territory but only 31% of its population. Namur is the capital and Charleroi the most populous city. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], Wallonia was second only to the United Kingdom in industrialization, drawing on extensive coal and iron deposits, and it was the more prosperous half of Belgium until the mid-20th century. Since [[World War II]] heavy industry has declined, and [[Flanders]] has surpassed Wallonia in wealth. The economic inequalities and linguistic divide between the two regions are a major source of political conflict and a factor in Flemish separatism. The Ardennes, a forested highland, covers the south and southeast. A German-speaking minority of less than 1% of the Belgian population lives in the east. Wallonia has been a member of the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie since 1980.
